name: Uran-9

placement_rationale.text: As an armed remote combat platform, Uran-9's representative position sits at close-reconnaissance depth (doctrine.md's 1-5km band) alongside the dismounted positions and direct-fire assets it's built to substitute for — a cannon/ATGM/flamethrower loadout only has tactical value at engagement ranges near the line itself. 2km is consistent with that role, independent of the source's own note that fielding has lagged the concept.

key_facts.label: Main armament
key_facts.value: 2A72 30mm automatic cannon, coaxial 7.62mm MG, Ataka ATGMs, Shmel-M rocket flamethrowers

characteristics: 2A72 30mm automatic cannon, coaxial 7.62mm MG, Ataka ATGMs, Shmel-M rocket flamethrowers
Strength: Most heavily armed Russian UGV design with a public combat-role concept (facility security, reconnaissance, engaging personnel/equipment)
Limitation: Despite pre-war development and claimed Syria/Ukraine deployment, has not achieved widespread battlefield use - a real system that never scaled
Estimated quantity available: Limited deployment; not widely fielded despite years of development
employment_notes: Illustrates the gap between demonstrated/exhibition capability and actual battlefield deployment that runs through Russian combat-UGV development generally, per the source's own framing
contrast_vs_traditional: Uran-9 is Russia's armed, remotely controlled answer to the same problem Ukrainian combat UGVs solve on the other side of the line: putting firepower into a contested position without putting a crew there, reflecting the doctrine.md-documented shift of the most casualty-heavy moments of an engagement onto unmanned platforms on both sides.
